title: UNH increases financial aid, awarding record $40 million to incoming class - Concord Monitor
content:
The Concord Monitor is a Pulitzer Prize winning daily newspaper and website located in the capital city of New Hampshire. The Concord Monitor is Central NH's dominant media with more than 70 percent household penetration. The Monitor is a key source of news and information for Concord, NH. Sign up for the Concord Monitor’s morning newsletter for essential news each day, and our contests and promotions list for special offers and giveaways. The incoming class attending the University of New Hampshire was awarded $40 million in financial aid, the most given in the university’s history. Last year, 88% of the freshman class received financial aid, with an average award of $12,400. This year, that average climbed to more than $16,000, with almost every enrolled student — 96% — receiving aid, according to university spokesperson Tania deLuzuriaga. The increase in aid was not due to more public funding, said Kimberly DeRego, vice provost of enrollment management. Rather, DeRego said, the university made changes to its guidelines around financial aid that allowed it to increase some of its merit and need-based scholarships. Additionally, more students who applied and decided to attend UNH this year were eligible for these scholarships: The class of 2030 had an average high school GPA of 3.7 and enrolled 322 students in UNH’s Hamel Honors and Scholars College, a 20% increase over last year, according to the university. DeRego said more students demonstrated greater need as well. Award-winning coverage on breaking news and today’s top stories in and around the Capital Region. From Arts and Life to Sports and Opinion you’ll have unlimited access to the Concord Monitor's content. Families have expressed concerns about affordability for years, DeRego said. Improving financial aid has been an ongoing effort for the university. “We lose a lot of students to out-of-state institutions because they’re able to give more financial aid,” deLuzuriaga said. “When you take cost out of the equation, they can pick the program that they feel like is really truly best for them.” Last year, in-state tuition at UNH was $19,202, according to the U.S. Department of Education’s College Navigator. Out-of-state tuition was $39,852. “We’re hoping that for our families, it helps them to realize college is attainable for more students,” DeRego said. “I think that’s our hope, and that’s why we do these policies.” Yasmeen is the education reporter at the Concord Monitor. content: Bedford native and University of New Hampshire alum Gabby DeAngelis is training for the World Skyrunning Championships. The competition will take place in Spain's Canary Islands. title: Seabirds on the Wing - University of New Hampshire
content: The Gulf of Maine is a literal marine hotspot, warming three times faster than ocean waters elsewhere over the past four decades. These changes affect marine life, including the distribution and abundance of fishes that other species, such as seabirds, depend on for food. UNH researchers studied how shifts in the populations of forage fish — fish species that are important sources of food — affect the ability of one seabird, the common tern, to forage efficiently in order to produce eggs and provide food for their chicks after hatching. While common terns are highly mobile and able to cover large distances, the study’s findings indicate that increased movement effort when prey is locally scarce does not improve chick diet or survival, highlighting the far-reaching effects of the changing marine environment. Having to fly farther to catch fish may negatively affect egg laying and tern chick survival. In a paper published in Movement Ecology, a research team led by UNH scientists Aliya Caldwell, Elizabeth Craig, and Nathan Furey, presents data on tern movement, reproductive productivity, and chick provisioning collected across four breeding seasons. Furey, associate professor of biological sciences in the College of Life Sciences and Agriculture, Caldwell, a biological sciences doctoral candidate in Furey’s lab, and Craig, director of seabird research at the Shoals Marine Lab and affiliate faculty of the department of biological sciences, worked on White and Seavey Islands at the south end of the Isles of Shoals. The islands are home to the site of the largest common tern breeding colony in the Gulf of Maine and are managed annually by Shoals Marine Laboratory researchers in collaboration with the New Hampshire Fish and Game Department. “Our results suggest that even though adult common terns can adjust their movements when forage fish locations shift, longer distance movements to find food may not improve chick survival rates,” says Caldwell. “The findings underscore the importance of implementing proactive management for foraging seabirds, as warming waters may increasingly lead to years of high foraging effort, poor diet, and low reproductive success.” The Gulf of Maine has historically been a rich hunting ground for common terns, boasting large populations of forage fishes such as herrings, hakes, and sand lances. These fishes are the right size and shape for terns to capture and ingest, with herrings and sand lances providing particularly high energy density. While there have always been annual variations in the exact amounts of fish available to the terns and the areas in which they congregate, the recent warming trends have led to significant shifts in abundance and location. Also, warmer water species such as Atlantic butterfish, a wide-bodied fish that most tern chicks are unable to swallow, are now moving into the Gulf. The Isles of Shoals are located about six miles off the New Hampshire coast. The researchers deployed solar-powered GPS tags on adult common terns to monitor their movements during the 2021–2024 breeding seasons. They also collected prey provisioning  — the actual prey fed to the chicks — and reproductive productivity data including egg laying and chick survival from nests within the colony. Their observations indicated that two of the years, 2022 and 2024, had ample forage fish availability near the White and Seavey Islands colony, while local prey availability was lower in 2021 and 2023, causing foraging movement effort to increase. During 2021 and 2023, the foraging trips extended to include the waters off central and southern Massachusetts, nearly 100 miles from the colony. Early-season access to prey is essential for egg laying, and common terns rely on energy from real-time food acquisition to produce eggs. The data showed that the years with plentiful nearby forage fish saw more eggs laid and much better chick survival than in the years that adults had to seek fish farther away. “Looking ahead, we recently received [National Science Foundation] funding to investigate the role of individual variations in foraging behavior — that is, do some birds move or feed differently than others?” says Furey. “Perhaps some birds can be flexible and change their diets or movements within a breeding season, with an impact on chick survival. In addition to common terns, Aliya will expand her work to include roseate terns, Arctic terns, great black-backed gulls, black guillemots, and Atlantic puffins at colonies throughout the Gulf of Maine.” The importance of the research is underscored by current projections that environmental changes will further accelerate shifts in forage fish communities. If the projections are accurate, increased foraging effort during breeding seasons may lead to increased movement effort and decreased reproductive success, threatening seabird populations in the Gulf of Maine and elsewhere. title: Justice Foreclosed? - University of New Hampshire
content: Every year, schools and government agencies join the nation in observing Constitution Day and Citizenship Day the week before and after Sept. 17, the anniversary of the signing of the Constitution. Federal courts participate by offering educational resources and experiences in their communities. Below, UNH associate professor of political science Susan Siggelakis pens a piece entitled "Justice Foreclosed?" This essay considers the Supreme Court case Pung v. Isabella County, Michigan. Here is the opinion. If you’ve lived in New Hampshire for any length of time, you may have heard people complaining about their property tax bill. Twice a year, homeowners receive the dreaded missive in the mail, perhaps procrastinating for a few weeks or months before reluctantly forking over thousands of dollars to their city or town government. Even if you live in an apartment, you will see this tax reflected in your ever-increasing rent bill as your landlord, too, pays this hefty exaction. Though it may seem that residents are paying simply for the privilege of living in their own places, the fact is that the proceeds from these local taxes pay for local schools, fire departments, libraries, road maintenance and other key municipal departments and services. Moving to another state is no solution. Throughout the United States, property taxes are a ubiquitous feature of modern life. Of course, in many cases property taxes may be discounted for senior citizens, veterans, or owners who chose to put some of their property in a conservation easement, for example. Yet, for almost all of us, it is our duty as good citizens to pay up, a civic act one that helps maintain and improve our quality of life. What happens if we don’t pay our property tax? One Michigan couple found out the hard way, with their dispute going all the way to the U.S. Supreme Court. Their dispute began in 2020. The Pungs, who had inherited their home from a deceased relation, lived full time in their dwelling and considered it their permanent home. In Michigan and numerous other states, (but not New Hampshire!), a vacation home or second property is taxed at a higher rate than a primary residence. For some disputed and unclear reasons their Isabella, Michigan county government taxed the Pungs’ home as if was a secondary property. The bill was $2,241.93. Though they attempted to clear this up, in the end the Pungs failed to persuade the tax officials that this was their primary residence. They also rejected several options offered by the county to end the stalemate. They refused to pay it. In the end, as is common throughout the states when people default on property taxes, the county foreclosed legally on the home. County officials later auctioned it off to the highest bidder for about $76,000, even though the home itself had been recently assessed as being worth $194,000. From the $76,000, the government took out the default amount, and returned the surplus, $73,766, to the Pungs. In doing so the county again complied with historical practice and state and local laws. The Pungs, having now lost their home, claimed that they should have received the surplus money from the $194,000 which was the assessed value of their home. This would have been about $192,000, much more than they received after the auction. Do the federal courts, applying the U.S. Constitution, have anything to say about this? Indeed they do. The Pungs were able to file their suit in federal district court, because they rested their argument on what is called a “federal question,” (i.e. a dispute about the meaning of a federal statute, a federal regulation or treaty, or the U.S. Constitution). First, they claimed that the Fourteenth Amendment’s due process clause had been violated because of the many procedural irregularities in the foreclosure procedures. For example, the Pungs claimed they did not receive the notice of foreclosure until after the county’s deadline, and that the $2,241.93 amount was not in the original tax bill that they had received. The 14th Amendment reads, “No state shall deprive any person of life, liberty or property without due process of law.” Except for being directed at the states instead of the national government, this replicates the Fifth Amendment’s provision. More important for this discussion is that the Pungs claimed the Takings Clause of the Fifth Amendment of the United States Constitution had been violated when they did not receive the surplus from a “fair market value” of the sale of their foreclosed home. That amendment reads in relevant part “[nor shall any person] be deprived of life, liberty or property without due process of law; nor shall private property be taken for public use, without just compensation.” The single district court judge, relying on various precedents, ruled against the Pungs, as did the three-judge panel of the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals. The Pungs then appealed to the United States Supreme Court, which granted the writ of certiorari to hear the case. Like the U.S. Court of Appeals, the U.S. Supreme Court is an appellate court, whose function is to ensure that courts below did not make any errors in interpreting and applying federal law. The Pungs had argued that centuries of “eminent domain” decisions, that is, instances when a state or city takes someone’s property for public use and just compensation is given, should guide the Court’s opinion. In centuries of legal opinions, the constitutional phrase “just compensation” has generally meant fair market value. An example of eminent domain would be when the state of New Jersey in the late 1960s took hundreds of houses adjacent to a stretch of the New Jersey Turnpike to widen the turnpike to accommodate increasing traffic in the late 1960s. It paid homeowners compensation based on the current, assessed value of their houses. Many homeowners were pleased with the ‘fair market value’ amount they received, as it allowed them to move to nicer homes elsewhere. If numerous judges upholding eminent domain takings have equated ‘just compensation’ with the fair market value of the property, then the same rule should apply here, they asserted. Unfortunately for the Pungs, the Court’s decision was unanimous, 9-0. It upheld the rulings of the two courts below on the constitutional issue surrounding the amount of the surplus. All ruled that the county had complied with the Takings Clause in returning the surplus from the foreclosed sale. The county was not constitutionally required to return a higher surplus from the assessed value of the house prior to its sale. The Court rejected the Pungs’ argument for three reasons: 1) their use of irrelevant eminent domain precedents (prior decisions involving the Takings Clause); 2) the problems the Pungs’ new constitutional rule would pose for municipal governance as well as other taxpayers; 3) the noncontroversial practice of foreclosure sales over the course of United States history. The Court made quick work of dismissing the eminent domain precedents, arguing that the Pungs were comparing apples to oranges. As Associate Justice Alito, writing for the Court commented, “what might be just in one context may not be just in another.’” Even in eminent domain cases, he noted, courts sometimes deviated from the fair market value rule and found different types of compensation to be “just,” for instance “when market value has been too difficult to find, or when its application would result in manifest injustice to owner or the public.” In addition, in eminent domain takings, homeowners have generally done nothing wrong, unlike delinquent taxpayers. The second main prong of the Court’s opinion was the practical concerns of local and state government: “Tax sales are meant to collect unpaid taxes without undue delay and administrative expense.” Were towns and cities required to sell foreclosed properties the way homeowners typically do, they would either have to sell the property themselves or hire a real-estate agent. In the interim before a full value sale, which would be uncertain and likely take many months, the municipality would be deprived of the unpaid taxes. If the town or city couldn’t or wouldn’t sell the foreclosed property, the new legal rule advocated by the Pungs would mean that the municipality would still have to pay the former owners the full market value, a cost which would ultimately be shouldered by local taxpayers. This would most likely be done by increasing residents’ property tax bills! Alito writes “so for taxpayers as a group, the demise of tax sales might be a most unwelcome development.” The third prong of the opinion rests on the Court’s opinion of both what happened in the past with tax sales, but also what didn’t happen: “Tax sales have been an accepted means for governments to collect debts since the earliest days of our nation. If the takings clauses had rendered these sales untenable, they would have presumably faded away….”. Although Associate Justices Clarence Thomas and Neil Gorsuch both agreed with the main ruling, they noted some irregularities. In a concurring opinion, Justice Thomas (joined by Gorsuch in part) asserted that the Court’s opinion neglected the many traditional practices and legal norms that had historically protected debtors’ property from egregious takings, as he characterized the one here. First, he noted that it was well-established that the government had to try and sell the taxpayer’s personal property before it could try and take land or buildings. This was especially important when a small debt might conceivably put a family out of their home. If these ‘chattels’ were sufficient to discharge the tax debt, then land and homes were off limits to the government. In fact, if the government took more than what was required to discharge the debt, the property owner could sue the government for trespass or trover (a common law action to recover property or receive equal compensation of said property). In the past, judges had generally scrutinized foreclosure proceedings carefully to make sure that parties were notified in timely, complete fashion. Thomas also asserts that, in many cases, judges tried to ensure that auction prices were as close to market value as possible. Anchoring the right to property in Anglo-American political and legal thought, he cites the famous British jurist William Blackstone statement that “the law of the land… postpones even public necessity to the sacred and inviolable rights of property.” Thomas concludes: “the government exists to protect property; property does not exist to support the government.” In the end, the Court only settled the constitutional question, which now becomes precedent, a guide for all judges around the country should they encounter a similar legal dispute between government and a property owner. It sent back down (remanded) the case back to the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals to deal with the Pungs’ particular claims of the allegedly unfair procedures employed by Isabella County. It is certainly possible that the county will be held to have violated the “due process” that it was required to afford the Pungs under the Fourteenth Amendment. But that’s a story for another Constitution Day! Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. All rights reserved.

title: This Dividend Stock Is Staging a Turnaround in 2026 and Pays More Than 2.4% - inkl
content:
For much of 2025, UnitedHealth Group (UNH) looked like a company under siege as higher medical costs and weaker margins rattled investors. UNH stock sold off sharply, and questions emerged around the company’s earnings outlook as well as the health of its long-standing growth story. That picture is starting to improve in 2026. UnitedHealth's latest results showed a clear turnaround in profitability as it generated $112 billion in revenue and $8 billion in earnings from operations. Management also raised the company's full-year adjusted EPS outlook to a range of $19.50 to $20 and increased its operating cash flow forecast to about $24 billion. Those moves suggest UnitedHealth sees its recovery as more than a short-term earnings rebound. This improving earnings and cash flow profile carries particular weight for dividend investors, as UnitedHealth now pays an annualized dividend of $9.28 per share, offering a yield above 2.4%. With shares rebounding from their 2025 lows, can UnitedHealth’s improving margins and cash generation support both continued dividend growth and further upside? Let’s take a closer look. Based in Eden Prairie, Minnesota, UnitedHealth Group operates UnitedHealthcare, its health-benefits arm, and Optum, which provides pharmacy benefits, care delivery, data, and technology services. With a market capitalization of $337 billion, the company serves consumers, employers, governments, care providers, and health plans across its insurance and services platforms. On Sept. 15, UNH stock closed the session at $375.93 per share. The stock has gained 15% year-to-date (YTD) and more than 11% over the past 52 weeks. UNH stock has a PEG ratio of 1.4 times, which is below the sector median of about 1.8 times. Meanwhile, the price-to-cash flow (P/CF) multiple of about 18 times is above the sector median of around 15 times. UnitedHealth currently pays a forward annual dividend of $9.28 per share, which equates to a 2.4% yield. Investors who owned UNH stock as of the Sept. 14 record date will receive a $2.32 quarterly payment on Sept. 22. That payout is backed by improving earnings momentum. On July 16, the company reported second-quarter 2026 results that included $112 billion in revenue. The figure came in slightly ahead of the $110.6 billion consensus estimate and was flat with the prior year. Meanwhile, adjusted EPS of $6.38 beat the $4.88 consensus estimate. UnitedHealth's medical care ratio was 86.7% for Q2, helped by product changes, improved medical management, and better-aligned pricing. This measure included $860 million of favorable prior-period development, mainly tied to 2026 service dates. UnitedHealthcare served 48.5 million consumers, generating $86 billion in revenue and $3.9 billion in earnings. Optum supported more than 120 million consumers, generated $65.7 billion in revenue, and delivered $4 billion in earnings in Q2. Operating margin expanded to 7.1% from 4.6% a year earlier, reflecting a meaningful improvement in profitability. That progress supported $8 billion of earnings from operations and a 4.9% net margin. Cash flow from operations was $11.1 billion, equal to 1.9 times net income, providing substantial coverage for the dividend. The debt-to-capital ratio was 41.2% as of June 30, 2026. Margin expanded 160 basis points year-over-year (YOY), adding support to UNH’s broader turnaround thesis. UnitedHealth Group is pairing its operational recovery with a larger commitment to shareholders. Management now expects to repurchase at least $5 billion of common stock in 2026, raising its original buyback target. The firm had already repurchased $4 billion of shares through mid-July. The company is also directing resources toward programs that could improve affordability, access, and member engagement over time. UnitedHealth’s partnership with University of Tennessee Health Sciences will expand health hubs into more Tennessee communities. The initiative connects residents with local support and resources that address health-related social needs. In July, UnitedHealthcare also introduced a new spending account benefit that gives eligible consumers greater flexibility in using health plan funds. The offering expands choices for qualified healthcare and everyday wellness expenses. In addition, UnitedHealthcare expanded child and family behavioral coaching access to 13 million commercial members. The program provides families with support for behavioral and emotional challenges beyond conventional insurance coverage. Together, these initiatives show how UnitedHealth is approaching its recovery on two fronts. The buybacks return excess capital to shareholders, while care access and engagement programs could help the company manage costs and strengthen member relationships over time. UnitedHealth Group is due to report its Q3 2026 results on Oct. 27. Analysts expect EPS of $4.03, up 38% YOY from earnings of $2.92 per share. On July 22, Bernstein kept a “Buy” rating on UNH stock and assigned a $512 price target, pointing to 35% potential upside from current levels. Around the same time, UBS reiterated its “Buy” rating and lifted its target to $490 from $460, citing a stronger-than-expected Q2 performance and improving Medicare Advantage trends. The broader Wall Street view remains constructive. UNH stock has a consensus “Strong Buy” rating among 26 analysts with coverage. The average price target of $480.81 points to potential upside of 27% from current levels. UnitedHealth’s 2026 turnaround looks increasingly credible. Improving margins, stronger cash flow, a larger buyback plan, and a $9.28 annual dividend provide tangible support for the UNH stock investment case. Wall Street also sees meaningful upside if Medicare Advantage trends and Optum’s recovery continue. Overall, the most likely path forward is further progress, although quarterly results may remain uneven. Support for socialism stronger among younger voters A July 29 University of New Hampshire poll showing that half of Vermonters view socialism positively — compared with 42% who view capitalism positively — suggests the word “socialism” has considerable appeal in Vermont. But a closer look at the poll shows that support for socialism, membership in the Democratic Socialists of America and the electoral value of a DSA endorsement are three different things. The July Green Mountain State Poll found 51% of Vermont residents had a very or somewhat positive view of socialism, while 31% viewed it negatively. Capitalism was evenly divided: 42% positive and 42% negative. Another 14% were neutral or had no opinion about socialism, compared with 12% for capitalism. That does not mean half of Vermonters identify themselves as socialists or support the Democratic Socialists of America. The poll asked separately about attitudes toward an ideology and attitudes toward a political organization. The distinction is especially clear in the DSA numbers. Just 2% of Vermonters said they currently belong to DSA and another 1% said they were former members. Half said they had heard of the organization and understood what it was, but 19% had heard of it without knowing much about it, 22% had never heard of it and 7% were unsure. In other words, about half of those surveyed did not claim a solid understanding of DSA, despite the relatively favorable statewide numbers for socialism itself. Among the 878 respondents who had heard of DSA, 47% viewed the organization positively, 31% negatively, 15% were neutral and 7% were unsure. The partisan divide was large: the poll reported that 71% of Democrats had positive feelings about DSA, while 89% of Republicans had negative feelings. Independents were almost evenly split, with 39% positive and 35% negative. The poll also tested whether a DSA endorsement would actually influence a vote. Among respondents familiar with DSA, 37% said an endorsement would make them more likely to support a candidate, while 30% said it would make them less likely. Another 26% said it would have little or no effect and 7% were unsure. Among self-described socialists, 86% said a DSA endorsement would make them more likely to vote for a candidate. That fell to 62% among progressives, 45% among liberals and just 9% among moderates. In a column set to be published this weekend, former Rep. Bob Stannard of Manchester (himself leaning left but not a socialist, despite incorrect description on yesterday’s edition – Editor) defined Capitalism and Socialism. Capitalism: “Capitalism is an economic system where private individuals and businesses own the tools, factories, and resources used to make goods, rather than the government. According to the International Monetary Fund, capitalism relies on private ownership, profit, and competition.” Socialism: “Socialism is an economic and political system where the community or the government owns and controls the major means of production—such as factories, tools, and large businesses—instead of private individuals. According to the general Socialism Definition & Meaning from Merriam-Webster, the core idea is that shared ownership helps distribute wealth more evenly and provides basic needs like healthcare and education to everyone.” Age may help explain why socialism performs comparatively well in Vermont. The poll found 60% of Vermonters ages 18 to 34 had a positive view of socialism, compared with 25% who viewed capitalism positively. Among those 35 to 49, socialism was viewed positively by 54%, compared with 31% for capitalism. The relationship reversed among older Vermonters. Among those ages 50 to 64, 49% viewed capitalism positively and 47% viewed socialism positively. Among residents 65 and older, capitalism led 56% to 44%. About half of Vermonters under 50 viewed capitalism negatively, according to UNH. The poll also provides an important limit on what “positive toward socialism” means. Socialism did not translate into comparable acceptance of communism. Only 11% of Vermonters viewed communism positively, while 73% viewed it negatively. Fascism was viewed negatively by 90%. The ideological cross-tabs sharpen the distinction further. Nearly all respondents who identified as socialists viewed socialism positively, as did 78% of progressives and 60% of liberals. Moderates were nearly evenly divided, while 91% of conservatives and 69% of libertarians viewed socialism negatively. Vermont also stood apart from its northern New England neighbors. UNH found 50% positive toward socialism in Vermont, compared with 35% in New Hampshire and 39% in Maine. DSA was viewed positively by 47% of Vermonters familiar with it, versus 30% in both New Hampshire and Maine. Taken together, the poll indicates that “socialism” has become a relatively positive political label for many Vermonters, particularly younger residents and people on the political left. It does not establish that a majority of Vermonters identify as socialists, belong to DSA, support a particular socialist economic program, or would vote for a DSA-backed candidate. The Green Mountain State Poll was conducted online July 15-20 by the UNH Survey Center. It included 1,119 Vermont residents and reported a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 2.9 percentage points. Results were weighted for sex, age, education, region and Vermont’s 2024 election results. title: Race to Replace Democrat Senator in New Hampshire Shifts Toward GOP - Newsweek
content: SCOTUS Blocks Mail-Ballot Restrictions, McConnell Senate Return, Trump Dismisses AI Concerns: The Bulletin, Sept. 15 SCOTUS Blocks Mail-Ballot Restrictions, McConnell Senate Return, Trump Dismisses AI Concerns: The Bulletin, Sept. 15 EU Ambassador Addresses Canada Becoming An Associate Member SCOTUS Blocks Mail-Ballot Restrictions, McConnell Senate Return, Trump Dismisses AI Concerns: The Bulletin, Sept. 15 The race to replace retiring Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen in New Hampshire has shifted toward Republicans, with The Cook Political Report moving the contest from Lean Democratic to Toss Up as former Republican Senator John Sununu and Democratic Representative Chris Pappas prepare for November's general election. The shift comes after newer polls show a seemingly competitive race between Sununu and Pappas. A University of New Hampshire (UNH) poll conducted in late August found Sununu at 45 percent and Pappas at 43 percent among likely voters. A Saint Anselm College poll conducted earlier that month showed Pappas leading Sununu 48 percent to 41 percent. The race has also attracted significant spending from national Republicans, who are on pace to hold a $20 million advantage in New Hampshire, Cook notes. "Sununu allies have already outspent pro-Pappas groups by almost a 2-1 margin," according to the forecaster. Meanwhile, midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during midterm elections. Republicans currently hold a narrow majority in the House and Senate. Former Vice President Kamala Harris narrowly won the state in the 2024 presidential election over President Donald Trump by under 3 percent. Newsweek reached out to Sununu and Pappas' campaigns via email on Tuesday for comment. Recent polling on the race has somewhat narrowed compared to earlier surveys. UNH had Pappas ahead of Sununu 49 percent to 42 percent in April and 47 percent to 44 percent in June. RealClearPolitics currently lists the contest as a Toss Up as well, with its polling average showing Pappas at 45.5 percent and Sununu at 41.5 percent. A September co/efficient survey shows the candidates now tied at 46 percent each. The poll adds that 9 percent are undecided. Pappas' favorability in the poll is 37 percent compared to an unfavorable rating of 51 percent and 13 percent have no opinion. Sununu's favorability rating in the poll is 41 percent compared to a 47 percent unfavorable rating, while 12 percent had no opinion. The poll surveyed 958 likely general election voters in the state from September 9-11, 2026, and has a margin of error of 3.15 percent. In the write-up on the race, Cook said in part, "When it comes to the Senate race, some Democratic polling has the race within the margin of error (though others have Pappas with a more comfortable lead) but GOP polling has shown the race tied or with Sununu ahead. It is possible that most of the undecided voters will ultimately break for Democrats, but it’s hard to forecast outcomes in the famously independently-minded state until the race fully engages." Craig Agranoff, Florida Atlantic University political professor, told Newsweek on Tuesday when asked if this is concerning for Democrats, "It’s a red flag because of the combination, not just one poll. You have a well-known Republican in John Sununu, an open Democratic seat, tightening surveys, and outside Republican money flowing in. That is how a Lean Democrat race becomes a toss up. It does not mean Democrats lose NH. It means they have to spend time and money here instead of putting all of it into flipping Republican seats." The latest shift is particularly significant because the Granite State has not elected a Republican senator since 2010. Sununu, who previously represented New Hampshire in the Senate, won the Republican nomination earlier this month, while Pappas won the Democratic nomination. Both candidates now face a general election campaign that is expected to receive significant national attention as Democrats seek to regain control of the Senate as Republicans hope to hold on. title: UNH Stock Breaks $380 Support as $350 and $300 Come Into Focus Despite Stronger Q2 Earnings UnitedHealth - FXLeaders
content: UnitedHealth’s strong earnings have failed to reverse the stock’s deterioration, with a break below $380 increasing the risk of a deeper decline toward $350 and $300. UnitedHealth delivered Q2 revenue and earnings beats while maintaining a medical loss ratio of 86.7%. The company also raised its full-year guidance, while analysts have continued to increase EPS estimates. However, those positives have failed to generate sustained buying interest. The disconnect between improving fundamentals and weakening price action is becoming increasingly concerning. UnitedHealth Group (UNH) stock is coming under renewed selling pressure despite stronger-than-expected second-quarter results and raised full-year 2026 guidance. The shares have been declining since July, when they failed to break through resistance above $460. Today’s move below $380 strengthens the bearish reversal and suggests sellers are gaining control. The break below $380 leaves the stock vulnerable to further losses. If buyers cannot quickly reclaim the level, $350 becomes the next major downside target, followed by the psychologically important $300 area. UnitedHealth remains a large healthcare company with a market capitalization of roughly $340 billion, a 2.45% dividend yield and an attractive 6.9% free-cash-flow yield. Yet those fundamentals have not prevented the technical breakdown. Unless UNH can recover above $380 and eventually challenge the failed $460 resistance zone, the bearish trend remains firmly intact.

When it comes to investing, there is no one-size-fits-all approach. Strategies vary based on numerous factors, including but not limited to investors’ risk tolerance, net worth, and age. When it comes to stock-picking, that last one is important. Conventional wisdom says that younger investors with longer horizons should focus on decades of exposure to growth stocks. Middle-aged investors may want to reduce their risk profile while seeking out a combination of growth and yield. Older investors tend to home in on income generation. While higher-volatility growth sectors like tech and communication services don’t necessarily fit the bill, some sectors offer something for every investor regardless of their age. The healthcare sector is one of those. And after an unremarkable start to the year, that corner of the market has been on a tear in the second half. Healthcare’s mix of high-growth drugmakers, defensive operators, and reliable dividend payers gives investors several ways to participate in the sector’s recent strength. Eli Lilly NYSE: LLY, which was founded in 1876, may not be the first thing to come to mind when younger investors think of growth stocks. Eli Lilly is the largest member of Big Pharma and the only one with a valuation north of $1 trillion. But because of its dynamic portfolio of diabetes, cancer, Alzheimer’s, and obesity drugs, it acts like a growth stock. Its lineup of obesity treatments is a particular driver of that growth. The company makes injectable Zepbound and Foundayo, a daily oral tablet for chronic weight management. So far this year, LLY has underperformed the market. But since its year-to-date (YTD) low on April 29, shares have rallied nearly 34%. Over the past five years, the stock has gained around 390%.Eli Lilly provides a modest dividend that yields 0.61%, or $6.92 per share annually, and has increased that payout for 11 consecutive years, with a five-year annualized growth rate of 15.18% and a healthy and sustainable payout ratio 23.22%. Grand View Research forecasts that the global obesity treatment market will undergo a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 22.3% from 2025 to 2030, while the global GLP-1 weight loss drug market will see an 18.5% CAGR during the same period. Its payout ratio of 62.11% is somewhat elevated and its five-year annualized dividend growth rate of 5.25% isn’t as impressive as the other two stocks on this list. title: Online Sports Betting Comes with a Cost, UNH Research Finds - University of New Hampshire
content: Being able to place a bet from virtually anywhere with just a few taps on a phone may be viewed as a convenience by some sports fans, but recent University of New Hampshire research shows that convenience may come at a cost. In a study led by Gorkem Turgut (G.T.) Ozer, assistant professor of decision sciences at UNH Peter T. Paul College of Business and Economics, researchers found that state legalization of online sports betting was associated with a 22.8% increase in calls to the National Problem Gambling Hotline, and a 3.1% increase in suicide rates. “Our key finding highlights a divide: the negative consequences manifest primarily when the activity shifts online,” Ozer says. “The widespread accessibility of mobile gambling coincided with a measurable uptick in problem gambling hotline calls and elevated suicide rates." When the researchers looked at different demographic groups, they found younger, unmarried and relatively less-educated men were most affected — a group previous research also identified as vulnerable to problem gambling. Ozer's research was recently published in Information Systems Research. While previous research has linked easier access to gambling with greater potential for harm, Ozer says there was little evidence showing just how much digital access could amplify those risks in the relatively new U.S. online sports betting market. To reach their findings, Ozer and study co-authors Brad Greenwood, professor of business at George Mason University, and Anandasivam Gopal, professor of business at Nanyang Technological University, analyzed problem gambling hotline calls and suicide rates across the U.S. as states legalized sports betting at different times. Because states differed in whether and when they legalized online betting and physical sportsbooks, the researchers were able to compare the effects of each form of legalization. The growing risks go beyond just the ease of placing a bet. The research notes that technology has changed the overall nature of sports betting. Consumers are no longer limited to traveling to a physical location to place a wager before a game starts. They can now bet live as a game unfolds or make proposition bets on individual moments and player performances — from whether a particular player will score a touchdown to how many fouls a basketball player will commit. “The business model of these platforms relies on sustained user participation,” Ozer says. “Integrating real-time feedback loops with unrestricted betting access creates an environment with a lower threshold for potential compulsive behavior.” While the rapid growth of sports betting has generated billions of dollars in revenue, along with tax revenue for states, Ozer says the research findings highlight potential societal costs that policymakers should consider alongside those economic benefits. “As online sports betting generates substantial state revenue, policy must actively mitigate its downstream harms,” Ozer says. “Such efforts may include ensuring better provider training, expanded mental health resources, and targeted outreach for high-risk groups.” The findings are also relevant for colleges and universities, Ozer says, because younger adults are among the groups most affected, and online betting platforms give students around-the-clock access. "Just as policymakers must weigh tax revenue against public harm, university leaders need to recognize these specific risk conditions and use empirical evidence to shape campus policies, digital guidelines, and student support programs," Ozer says. Online sports betting fits into Ozer's broader research interest in how digital platforms can influence compulsive behavior. He is particularly interested in how unpredictable rewards, social feedback and game-like features can create a cycle that keeps users coming back — and how, when those behaviors occur across millions of users, their effects can grow from individual concerns into broader societal issues. Ozer recently received part of a $2.6 million award to continue researching the financial and household impacts of sports betting. He will partner with other researchers to examine how people’s financial health changes when they move between states with different sports betting laws, including potential changes in credit health and financial distress. Sports betting is now legal in 39 states and Washington, D.C., and Ozer says the continued growth of online betting and prediction markets is making it an increasingly important area. "Combined with a rapid shift toward younger demographics, identifying further downstream implications to guide policy is more critical than ever," Ozer says. title: UDay Introduces Students to More Than 200 Groups and Organizations - University of New Hampshire
content: After rain forced a one-week postponement, the weather delivered a beautiful afternoon and the usual huge crowd filled the heart of campus for the annual University Day (UDay) celebration Sept. 10, as one of UNH's most anticipated fall traditions introduced new and returning Wildcats to more than 200 student clubs and campus organizations. An enthusiastic crowd of students, staff, faculty, and Durham community members filled the street and Thompson Hall lawn for the UDay community picnic, which featured a performance by the UNH marching band, a variety of food options, and a throng of student groups and organizations eager to recruit new participants. The event is one of the best ways for students to explore the wide array of offerings available on campus while making new connections with fellow Wildcats.
